name: Toki Pona rules
source: Toki Pona by Sonja Lang (Toki Pona: The Language of Good, 2014; the 120 words of the first book, 137 with the 2021 dictionary). Typed in from Claude's memory of the grammar; the examples are Claude's own and short. Not checked against the book.
use: Phase 7: sets Hao-shuo-de beside another minimal language on the same points (word order, how a sentence is joined, how a question is asked). The `hsd` field says what Hao-shuo-de does, left empty for the author.

items.rule: Words never change: no plural, no tense, no case.

example.en: The person is good. / The people are good.

items.rule: Subject, verb, object, in that order.
The word li comes between the subject and the verb, except when the subject is exactly mi (I, we) or sina (you).

example.en: She is good. I am good.

items.rule: The word e marks the object.
A describing word follows the word it describes; adjectives and nouns are not told apart.
The word pi groups a longer describing phrase so it modifies the head as a whole.

example.en: A house of strange water (a bar).

items.rule: A short list of words used before a noun to say place, direction, tool, likeness or cause: lon, tawa, tan, kepeken, sama.
The word la ends a context phrase (time, condition) and starts the main sentence.

example.en: At this time I am fine.

items.rule: The word ala after a word makes it negative.
A yes/no question repeats the verb with ala between: X ala X.
A question word (seme) goes in the place of the answer, not moved to the front.
The word o marks a command or a wish.
A few number words (ala 0, wan 1, tu 2, luka 5, mute 20, ale 100) are added up; a number follows the noun it counts.
The word en joins subjects, anu means 'or'; the word taso is 'but'.
A word does the work of noun, verb or adjective by its place in the sentence.

example.en: The food is good. I eat.

items.rule: Three pronouns: mi, sina, ona; the number is told by context or by mute.
A name follows a common word and is written with a capital; it is the one thing that is not a Toki Pona word.
Time is said with a time word in a context phrase, never on the verb.
About 120 words in the first book (137 in the 2021 dictionary); new ideas are said by joining the words.
